issues.item: Triggers: Power Imbalance: Being in a situation where someone has power over me
issues.explanation: The trigger 'being in a situation where someone has power over me' is hard to reconcile with the stated trauma type of natural disaster and with the rest of the profile, which otherwise emphasizes alarm/reactivity and fragmented recall rather than interpersonal domination or coercion. For this trauma type, this item introduces an implausible trigger theme not supported elsewhere in threat, memory, or appraisals.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
issues.explanation: Avoiding hospitals/ambulances/physical examinations is not well supported by the rest of the profile for a natural-disaster trauma. There are no memory or threat items involving injury treatment, medical rescue, or bodily harm, so this strategy appears to target a symptom theme not represented elsewhere. In contrast, the profile is centered on generalized alarm, shouting, unpredictability, and fragmented memory.

issues.item: Self-Harm: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings
issues.explanation: Self-harm is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile and trauma context: the other selected items describe a classic hyperarousal/re-experiencing natural-disaster PTSD presentation with avoidance and overeating, but no accompanying items suggest the kind of shame, self-punitive appraisal, dissociative affect regulation, or broader emotion-dysregulation pattern that would make physical self-harm clinically coherent here. It stands out as addressing a symptom process not otherwise represented in the five components.

Alcohol smell is not impossible, but in this profile it is weakly anchored to the reported trauma type and the rest of the item set. The other triggers (unpredictability, shouting) fit a danger/hyperarousal formulation, whereas alcohol smell implies a very specific sensory trauma cue that is not supported by the memory or threat items. Given a natural-disaster index trauma, this trigger is difficult to explain clinically without additional corroborating content.

vignette:
Hassan had spent most of his adult life in situations where a split second mattered, but the event that changed him was different from the explosions and controlled detonations he knew at work. Years earlier, while visiting relatives in a coastal area, he was caught in a sudden storm surge that turned roads into moving water within minutes. One moment he was trying to get people into higher ground; the next, the noise of slamming doors, shouted warnings, and the roar of water all seemed to collide at once. In the middle of that chaos he lost track of where his younger cousin had gone, and for hours afterward he carried the sickening belief that he had failed to keep him safe. Even now, when Hassan tried to remember the flood, the memory would not come back as a whole. He found himself pushing it away before he could fully recall it, getting only fragments: mud on concrete, someone shouting his name, the taste of panic, his own anger rising hard and hot when he thought of how quickly everything had gone wrong. What remained was an incomplete picture, and the missing parts made the whole event feel even more unbearable. The more those fragments broke through, the more everyday things in his life started to take on the feel of warnings; a garage door rattling, a radio crackling in his truck, or a voice suddenly raised at work could all seem to carry the flood inside them.

Afterward, Hassan became intensely reactive to anything that echoed that day’s unpredictability. A sudden bang in the neighborhood, a shout across a street, or an unexpected change in a plan could hit him like a warning that danger was already unfolding. Living with that sense that danger might be present at any moment, he began to read the world as full of possible signals, so that even ordinary noises or interruptions could tip into something he felt he had to watch closely. In those moments his body reacted before he had time to think: his shoulders tightened, his chest went rigid, and he would find himself scanning for threat before he even knew what had set him off. He often reacted as if he were in danger when nothing was actually wrong, and the reaction was so immediate that it sometimes seemed to him like his body knew something his mind had not yet caught up to. The same cues also pulled at the broken memory itself. A loud noise in the garage, a neighbor yelling, or the unpredictability of a sudden alarm would bring back only pieces of the flood, and those fragments were enough to leave him flooded with rage and dread, as if the rest of the scene were waiting just out of reach.

To keep himself from being overtaken by that feeling, Hassan began structuring his life around control. He kept his mind occupied all the time, filling every spare moment with chores, television, phone calls, or work tasks, and when the tension still rose he would eat excessively to blunt it. He also avoided anything that could be stressful, declining extra responsibilities, steering away from crowded places, and trying to keep his days as orderly as possible. Yet these efforts did not calm him for long. At home, the more he tried to stay busy and out of harm’s way, the more easily he seemed to catch himself on edge, listening for a shout outside or a harsh sound in the street. At work, where he was a bomb disposal technician, he could no longer dismiss the sharp intake of breath he felt when a radio crackled unexpectedly or a colleague raised his voice. The very strategies he used to protect himself left him more primed to notice danger, and once he noticed it, he felt the need to withdraw further, making his world smaller and more guarded.

That narrowing also fed back into the memory. The more Hassan avoided stress and kept himself distracted, the less he allowed the flood to be thought about directly, and the more the event stayed locked in fragments. When a trigger did break through, he would catch himself in a brief flashback-like moment, suddenly feeling as if he were back in that surge of water and noise, and the return of the scene would be partial and jagged rather than coherent. Each partial recall came with the same surge of rage and alarm, which made him shove the memory away again. In turn, the pushed-away memory made his reactions harder to understand and more frightening: he knew only that certain noises, shouts, and sudden changes could set off the whole sequence. Because unpredictability felt especially dangerous, he became even more alert for it, watching for signs that something was about to go wrong. That vigilance meant he was more likely to notice the next shout, the next loud bang, the next abrupt interruption, and each one reinforced his sense that threat could appear without warning.

By the time Hassan sought help, the pattern had started to affect his marriage and his work. His wife had noticed how often he ate in the evenings and how often he seemed mentally elsewhere, as if he were using every ounce of effort to keep himself occupied and away from whatever might stir him up. He had begun turning down social plans and staying home more, because even small disruptions felt risky. What finally brought him to treatment was the growing fear that his reactions were no longer just uncomfortable but could interfere with the careful judgment his job required. Hassan came hoping to regain some control over his mind and body, but he was most afraid that one sudden noise, one unexpected shout, might pull him back into that unfinished day before he could stop it.

violations.explanation: The vignette shows the memory being brought back by cues, but it does not clearly state that the memory itself causes or generates new triggers.
The vignette shows threat leading to heightened vigilance and fear, but it does not explicitly convey that threat produces triggers or triggering cues.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Memory → Triggers: The vignette shows the memory being brought back by cues, but it does not clearly state that the memory itself causes or generates new triggers.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Threat → Triggers: The vignette shows threat leading to heightened vigilance and fear, but it does not explicitly convey that threat produces triggers or triggering cues.
  e.g. "Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been."
  e.g. "The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each one confirming what her body already believed."
  e.g. "Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading."
